items.title: Pope Leo on spiritual life: 2 risks to avoid and 2 things to do
items.summary:
“In Christ there are not two missions, one spiritual and one social,” Leo XIV told participants in the plenary assembly of the Dicastery for Promoting Integral Human Development. “There is a single mission, the messianic one: He is the Savior of every human being and of the whole person.” This is a timely reminder not just for members of the dicastery, but for all of us. During his address — given on November 26 — the Holy Father goes on to describe two risks we face in living out the Gospel message. On the one hand, there is the risk “of reducing the Gospel to a mere social or welfare program.” At its most extreme, this means seeing Jesus not as the Son of God who came to save us from our sins and transform our lives from within, making us children of God, but merely as a social activist. This strips the Gospel “of Read More…

items.title: This diocese is creating a tiny village for elderly homeless
items.summary:
In December 2025, Pensacola-based civic entrepreneur Jarah Jaquay posted to Facebook about his Florida diocese:   The Diocese of Pensacola-Tallahassee — and some very generous local donors — have put their money where their mouths (and their treasure where their hearts) are. #TrinityVillage isn’t a concept study or a slogan. It’s nine real homes, nearly complete, for senior citizens experiencing housing insecurity. A first-of-its-kind pilot in #Pensacola. Concrete, wood, roofs, doors — and dignity. This is what #YIGBY (Yes In God’s Backyard) looks like when it’s more than a buzzword. “Yes In God’s Backyard” is state legislation allowing for flexible residential zoning that applies to land owned by religious institutions. It allows affordable housing to be built on their property (with certain restrictions, varying state by state). Washington state was the first to pass the initiative in 2019, followed by Oregon in 2021. It passed in California and Minnesota in 2023, Maryland and Hawaii in Read More…

items.summary:
Bending his head slightly, Paul Knight speaks into the microphone with a cadence, “God is good …”   “All the time,” his listeners respond, taking up the familiar call-and-response. “All the time, God is good.” This is how the brief video recording of Knight’s testimony begins. He spoke at St. George’s Church in Taunton in southwest England’s Somerset County on October 11 after the 9:15 am Mass.  The story he shared began less than a mile away, at Musgrave Park Hospital, where in May 2026, Knight was hospitalized for meningitis. He had received Holy Communion and the Anointing of the Sick from a priest chaplain and was comforted by sacramentals like the Miraculous Medal. items.title: A Spanish farm sent 150 turkeys to the Vatican’s lunch for the poor
items.summary:
On November 22, Pope Leo XIV sat down to lunch with more than 1,300 people experiencing poverty in the Paul VI Audience Hall — the 10th edition of the World Day of the Poor lunch that Pope Francis established in 2017. What most guests didn’t know was that the turkeys on the table had arrived from the dehesa charra, the oak woodland of Salamanca, Spain, prepared according to a recipe drawn from one of the most celebrated cookbooks in Renaissance history. Fundación Cascajares, a Spanish artisanal turkey producer based in the Castile and León region, donated 150 birds to the Vatican for the occasion. The turkeys were raised at the foundation’s estate in Aldealgordo, Salamanca, on the characteristic oak pastures of the region, and prepared using a recipe inspired by the culinary traditions of the 16th-century papal kitchen — specifically the work of Bartolomeo Scappi, whose 1570 Opera dell’arte del cucinare remains one of the Read More…

items.title: Workers restoring Hagia Sophia found a vast hidden world beneath it
items.summary:
For centuries, Istanbulites spoke of tunnels beneath the Hagia Sophia. Now, a network of underground passages, chambers, and water channels has been uncovered beneath the great 6th-century basilica during an ongoing restoration project, Turkish authorities announced on November 20. Some of what has been found predates the building itself, which has stood since 537. The discovery, however, is not entirely a surprise. Beyond long-standing urban legends, underground infrastructure, including a four-room Roman burial structure, was already known from excavations in the 1940s. But the scale of what is now emerging goes well beyond what had been documented. So far, nearly 3,000 tons of debris have been removed, 420 meters of tunnels cleared, and six chambers connected by nine tunnels identified. The longest single tunnel runs approximately 180 meters. Turkish Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy has suggested the full network may extend to roughly 9 kilometers. The tunnels served practical purposes: housing terracotta water Read More…

items.title: From Alaska, a captivating way to pray the Divine Office
items.summary:
The Divine Office, or the Liturgy of the Hours, is a daily rhythm of prayer that unites Christians around the world — but although priests and members of religious life pray it daily, many Christians might not even know about it. This ancient and powerful prayer gets its due attention in a beautiful new book. The Illuminated Soul: Praying the Liturgy of the Hours with Sacred Art illustrates the text of the Benedicite (Daniel 3:57-88) and pairs it with essays and questions for contemplation. The Benedicite is the canticle for Morning Prayer in the Divine Office every other Sunday and on solemnities and feast days.  The author, Charles Rohrbacher, told Aleteia that the book grew out of his own experience praying the Divine Office over the past five decades. Rohrbacher, a Catholic deacon, artist, and iconographer who lives in Alaska, found that the Benedicite’s invocation of the cosmos “took hold of his imagination” each time Read More…

items.title: ‘She was so not regretful about killing her husband’: the Iranian film that shines a light on blood money and retributive justice
items.summary:
The co-director of An Eye for an Eye, Tanaz Eshaghian, reveals how she came to make a documentary about a woman facing the threat of execution from her husband’s family – as sanctioned by sharia law

“Even though I was raised here,” says the Iranian-American film-maker Tanaz Eshaghian from her home in New York, “I was brought up with the understanding that there are things that you do and things that you don’t do.” Take her 2006 autobiographical feature, Love Iranian-American Style, about her experience of dating in her 20s, which was, she says, “about how I was supposed to marry a nice Iranian man and stay a virgin”. But by the time she’d graduated from Brown University in Rhode Island “that ship had sailed”, she laughs.

Since Love Iranian-American Style, she has made equally taboo-breaking documentaries about a women’s prison in Afghanistan (Love Crimes of Kabul, 2011), trans people in Iran (Be Like Others, 2008) and disabled teenagers in Pakistan (As Far As They Can Run, 2022). And with each new project, the duality of her heritage (Eshaghian emigrated to the US not long after the Iranian revolution when she was six) has spurred her to focus eastwards, closer to where she was born. “When you’ve been raised in the west you can see how similar the thinking is,” Eshaghian says of the similarities she’s found there: “the conservative thinking, the place of women, what’s allowed, what’s important”.

Continue reading...

items.title: Publisher’s Note: A personal message of thanks and an update on our year at Crux
items.summary:
As winter draws closer and the festive season begins, we at Crux  want to take a moment to share with you the journey we’ve been on this past year.

First though, as publisher, I try to stay behind the scenes and keep a low profile, but today I’ve decided to share a bit more about myself. 

There is a selfish reason behind this: In the coming weeks, when you hear from me, I want you to know who I am and what I stand for. I want you to understand why I’ve taken on the challenging task of preserving John Allen Jr.’s legacy and securing Crux ’s future by rebuilding it into a thriving, sustainable media organization.

I also want you to know I am human, not a robot sending out notes written by Artificial Intelligence (AI). That may sound ridiculous, but many of you have no idea how much of what you read these days—even in credible newspapers—is created with AI.

Like many Americans, I’m planning a cozy Thanksgiving meal with my family. While this may seem easy, two things make it a little tougher than average for me.

First, while I was born and raised in Cambridge, Massachusetts, I now live in Copenhagen with my Danish husband. Imagine trying to fit a giant turkey into an adorable, European-sized oven! I say this in jest, especially as I dislike cooking. To me, Thanksgiving is all about giving thanks and sharing precious time with family and friends. The food is just the bait to get everyone to the table.

This brings me to the second challenge: Getting the family together.

Our beloved daughter began studying in America this year. I won’t go into specifics, but let’s just…

items.title: They belong to Jerusalem’s past and present: meet the African Palestinians
items.summary:
Despite militarisation, occupation and marginalisation, African culture prevails in the Old City, something I discovered first-hand when I visited

  • Don’t get The Long Wave delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

In occupied East Jerusalem, I met an often overlooked community: African Palestinians. This week, I explore their unique history, and how they are, in a classic diaspora fashion, integrated and marginalised in equal measure.

There are about 450 African Palestinian people in occupied East Jerusalem, mostly living in the historical buildings of the Old City, near al-Aqsa mosque. That mosque, the third holiest site in Islam after those in Mecca and Medina, is the reason they are there. While Christians make up a small part of the African Palestinian population, most African Palestinians descended from Muslim pilgrims who came to East Jerusalem in the early 20th century (before Israeli occupation), and stayed either to tend to the mosque, or to continue Islamic practice and devotion within the city’s religious ecosystem.

Continue reading...

items.title: Church in India mourns passing of beloved archbishop, a force for peace and reconciliation
items.summary:
Crux

MUMBAI – The Catholic Church in India lost a senior prelate on Wednesday, who was a prominent figure on the national stage despite his dislike of the limelight, and a force for reconciliation in the country’s troubled northeast for many decades.

Archbishop Thomas Menamparampil, a member of the Salesians of Don Bosco, died in the early hours of Wednesday, Nov. 25, at AIG Hospital, Hyderabad, of complications following a liver illness. He was 90 years old.

Cardinal Oswald Gracias, emeritus of Mumbai, told Crux Now Menamparampil was “a fearless bridge-builder” who worked tirelessly for peace, reconciliation, and Christian unity.

“He never sought to get attention to himself,” Gracias said. “He always stayed out of the center. He didn’t draw attention to it, but he did all the work.”

The 81-year-old cardinal had known the late archbishop since they were both young priests, and they worked together for many decades.

Gracias especially recalled Menamparampil’s courageous work for peace and understanding in the northeast Indian state of Manipur, where religious identity intersects with deep-rooted and complex ethnic, social, and economic conflicts.

A statement from the Catholic Bishops’ Conference of India recalled Menamparampil’s many successful efforts to bring relief to those suffering the effects violence and foster reconciliation.

The CBCI and Gracias remember Menamparampil as a frank and tireless advocate for Christians of all denominations and a respected voice capable of engaging Hindus and Muslims as an honest broker in disputes between those communities.…
items.t: Church in India mourns passing of beloved archbishop, a force for peace and reconciliation

Pope Leo XIV has assigned two major topics to the International Theological Commission (ITC), which he received in audience on Wednesday, November 25, at the Apostolic Palace: Apostolic Tradition, and the cultural forms through which faith is transmitted across generations and cultures. Speaking to the commission shortly before his weekly general audience, the Pope outlined the work that will occupy them over the next five years: two major themes rather than the three that have been standard in recent mandates. The first theme is Apostolic Tradition: the transmission of Christ’s message through the apostles and the Church that followed them. items.title: Spain’s World Cup hero to receive prestigious faith-sharing prize
items.summary:
Ferran Torres, the scorer of Spain’s winning goal in the 2026 World Cup final, has been given an award for the public display of his Catholic faith.

Spain’s Asociación Católica de Propagandistas (ACdP), through its Fundación Universitaria San Pablo CEU , awarded Torres the CEU Ángel Herrera Prize.

Established in 1997, the Herrera Prize recognizes people inside and outside the university who promote the improvement of society and the common good.

Torres’ award, which he will receive Jan. 18, 2027, was within the category of the dissemination of Catholic culture.

A statement highlighted Torres’ “contribution to the visibility of the Catholic faith from elite sport, as well as his ability to transmit Christian values ​​naturally and coherently to millions of people.”

“I’ve never tried to convey anything extraordinary,” Torres said upon receiving news the prize would go to him. “I simply to be myself,” the soccer star said, “and remain true to the values ​​that have guided me since childhood.”

“The fact that this can have a positive impact on others is something that makes me especially happy,” the Paris Saint-Germain striker added.

The jury that awarded him the prize praised Torres for “giving visibility to the Catholic faith from one of the areas with the greatest projection and influence in today’s society.”

During the World Cup, Torres was vocal about his faith and the inspiration it gave him throughout his soccer career.

After he scored the winning goal against Argentina in the dying embers of the final, he gave thanks to God. Throughout the tournament, he faced…

items.title: The day St. Peter’s Basilica hosted its first council
items.summary:
On the morning of December 8, the feast of the Immaculate Conception, torrential rain makes the streets of Rome nearly impassable. Yet even before the first cold light of dawn, a feverish excitement takes hold around St. Peter’s Basilica. “A multitude of pilgrims from every nation have come to join the Romans in welcoming the Council on its opening day,” observes Father Léon Dehon, a French priest with a journalist’s instincts who is among the crowd. The rain has not prevented the 744 council fathers from gathering in a chapel above the basilica’s vast atrium, specially prepared for the occasion. items.title: Our review: The Story of St. John Henry Newman
items.summary:
The latest film from Lumine Studios, Lead Kindly Light: The Story of Saint John Henry Newman, brings to life the rich history of Newman’s formative years and exactly what he endured for truth, beauty, and goodness, which brought about a movement that still shines today in England and the world. Directors Gustavo Letie and Julia Sondermann have done a marvelous job of bringing Newman’s early writings to life, particularly those about his path toward God and eventually the Catholic Church. They walk in the steps of Newman at his favorite place in all the world: Oxford. The film was shot across multiple countries and with multiple theologians, to give various perspectives of Newman’s journey. It shares his famous 1833 hymn/poem, “Lead, Kindly Light amid the encircling gloom,” for which the film is named, as the tipping point to Catholicism. What many people perhaps do not realize is what Newman sacrificed on his path to God Read More…

items.title: Apple’s Emmy-winning ad celebrates the joy of being ordinary
items.summary:
There are certain things that every university student should be entitled to: falling hopelessly in love with someone who barely knows they exist, going to parties they might regret the next morning, and occasionally sleeping through a lecture because of that party. And, of course, the right to be spectacularly unimpressive from time to time, to fade into the crowd and bask in the joy of being completely and utterly ignored. Which is why Apple’s Emmy-winning film I’m Not Remarkable is such a treat. Instead of presenting students with disabilities as inspirational heroes simply for getting through the day, it celebrates their right to be just like everybody else. And it does so with a fabulous musical number, plenty of humor, and a rather infectious sense of fun. Directed by Kim Gehrig, with original music from Tony Award-winning composer Tim Minchin, the film won the 2026 Emmy for Outstanding Commercial. Its stars aren’t professional actors Read More…

items.title: Pope Francis’s diary reveals encounters with the devil and a fight against control
items.summary:
Extracts from the private diary of Pope Francis are set to be released across the world, made from a collection of notes he made between 1992-2024.

The Private Diary of Pope Francis , edited by Francis’ longtime friend and collaborator Cardinal Victor Manuel Fernández offers insight into the former pope’s intense inner life, revealing mystical encounters with Jesus and the devil, and a battle against a desire to control. 

Written in a calendar used as a notebook, the entries begin in 1992 when Francis was auxiliary bishop of Buenos Aires, and the final entry is Aug. 18, 2024, when he was pope.

The book will be released in several languages, including English.

According to the diary, Francis had three encounters with the devil, two when he was in Buenos Aires and one following a disastrous trip to Chile in 2018 as pope.

In the first encounter, Francis recalled sitting in a car and seeing the “threatening yet seductive” gaze of the devil.

The second was in a Carmelite chapel, and Francis used a rosary and an invocation of the Virgin Mary to protect himself.

During the Chile trip, Francis came under heavy fire for his discrediting of victims of sexual abuse, and after being questioned on the flight home by journalists, he commissioned an investigation. 

“A few days after returning to Rome, I was in a meeting. I saw him and heard his voice, triumphant possessing everything. ‘Now I’ve gotten everything I wanted’,” Francis said in a Jan. 24, 2021 entry. 

“Just as I can’t forget his eyes from the previous two, in this case, I can’t forget the powerful raspiness of his…
items.t: Pope Francis’s diary reveals encounters with the devil and a fight against control

Pope Francis wrote in his diary of encountering the devil and said he saw the “gates of hell” when he realised how serious a clerical sexual abuse scandal was, according to excerpts published on Tuesday.

The late Argentinian pontiff’s innermost thoughts, reflections and fears have been revealed in The Private Diary of Pope Francis, a book curated by his close aide cardinal Victor Manuel Fernández and being published globally in several languages.

items.title: Leo XIV wants new Swiss Guard barracks to honor tradition
items.summary:
Pope Leo XIV wants the new Swiss Guard barracks to be a place where Swiss traditions are passed down. He made the point on Monday, November 23, to those overseeing the renovation of the Vatican’s military housing. Expressing his hope that construction will soon begin, he thanked those who have worked for years on a project intended to serve future generations. Established in 2016, the Foundation for the Renovation of the Barracks of the Pontifical Swiss Guard is responsible for a massive project to rebuild the housing and infrastructure used by the Pope’s soldiers. The current barracks, built in the 19th century, are in poor condition. In recent years, the foundation has focused on raising the funds needed for the work. Addressing the foundation’s members and donors, the Pontiff praised their “patience and tenacity” and their efforts in “knocking on many doors.” Initially estimated at 45 million Swiss francs, the budget has since climbed to Read More… 

Leo XIV wants new Swiss Guard barracks to honor tradition
items.t: Leo XIV wants new Swiss Guard barracks to honor tradition

items.title: Science has good news for the faithful as they age!
items.summary:
Your average churchgoing grandmother could probably tell you a thing or two about the benefits of faith in old age. But now scientists have decided to investigate the matter, and it turns out Granny might have been onto something all along. Does faith help us enjoy a happier old age? Well, according to new research, it certainly seems to be associated with a better quality of life. And while Granny might be tempted to give the scientists a knowing smile, the findings are genuinely interesting, especially as more of us are living longer. Researchers from the University of Padua in Italy examined 21 studies involving 5,664 people aged between 60 and 104, looking at the relationship between religious or spiritual beliefs and wellbeing. Their findings, published in PLOS Aging and Health and reported by CNN, revealed a positive association between faith and quality of life, as well as overall life satisfaction. Science has good news for the faithful as they age!
items.t: Science has good news for the faithful as they age!

items.title: Meet Giulia Gabrieli, the Church’s newest 14-year-old venerable
items.summary:
On November 21, 2026, Pope Leo XIV officially recognized the heroic virtues of Giulia Gabrieli, thus declaring her “venerable.” This is an important step in the beatification and canonization process, as it verifies that Giulia lived a heroic life of virtue and that her example is worthy of imitation. The next step in her process to being declared a saint is for two miracles to be confirmed through her intercession. The first confirmed miracle will lead to her beatification, and the second to her canonization. She joins an ever-growing group of young people who have died in the 21st century and who are being considered for canonization. Born in Bergamo, Italy on March 3, 1997, Giulia was very active in her parish growing up, and received the sacrament of confirmation in 2009. items.title: Inspiration for a healthier swap on the Thanksgiving table
items.summary:
When Ellyn Caruso got a diagnosis of breast cancer, she leaned on her lifelong Catholic faith to stay hopeful and persevering — and was inspired to write a cookbook with healthier swaps to help others. Today, “profoundly grateful to have a second chance at a healthier life,” Caruso is on a mission to “inspire others to take charge of their lifestyle, and to arm more survivors with ideas and practical ways to thrive,” she told Aleteia. Her book, Forkfuls of Flavor: Mediterranean-inspired Dishes for Breast Cancer Thrivership, available on Amazon and at Walmart, has lots of clever ideas for your Thanksgiving table — or any time of year. Keep reading for our conversation with Caruso, and a healthy recipe from her cookbook for your Thanksgiving menu. In what ways did your Catholic faith inspire you to write your cookbook and to keep a positive and purposeful outlook throughout your cancer fight? At the age of Read More…

items.title: Myanmar has been found guilty of genocide. Should Israel be worried? – podcast
items.summary:
The international court of justice has for the first time ruled that a state has committed genocide. Yasmin Ullah explains what it means for the Rohingya people, while Kaamil Ahmed lays out how the case unfolded

For seven years, Yasmin Ullah had been part of the delegation arguing that Myanmar had committed genocide – one of the gravest human rights crimes – against Rohingya Muslims.

The genocide has directly affected Yasmin and her family. Last week she was in court to hear the international court of justice’s landmark verdict against Myanmar. “I was really kind of pinching myself. It felt like we were all able to breathe again,” she tells Annie Kelly.

Continue reading...

items.title: Pope appeals for peace on Christ the King, dines with Rome’s poor
items.summary:
Pope Leo XIV renewed his appeal for peace around the globe on Sunday, calling on leaders in positions of responsibility to work for equitable solutions to conflicts.

Addressing pilgrims and tourists in St. Peter’s Square for the Angelus on Sunday, the pontiff called the faithful to prayer “for the victims of the many conflicts that, sadly, continue to sow death and suffering throughout the world.”

“Let us pray for those in positions of responsibility,” Leo also said, “that they may commit to finding solutions for reconciliation and peace without delay.”

Pope Leo XIV greets pilgrims and tourists from the window of the Apostolic Palace in the Vatican on Sunday, 22 Nov. 2026. Image ©Vatican Media 

Peace has been a key motif of Leo’s pontificate, and he has prayed for an end to armed conflict in many of the world’s trouble spots, but his appeal this Sunday was global in scope and came on the Solemnity of Christ the King.

In remarks ahead of the traditional noonday Marian devotion, Leo recalled the intention of his predecessor, Pope Pius XI, who established the feast day in 1925, as the world slowly recovered from the horror of World War I.

“ In an era marked by tensions and conflicts,” Leo said, “my predecessor wished to emphasize that the Lord of history is the King of peace and justice for all the peoples of the world.”

“As a pilgrim through the centuries,” the pontiff also said, “the Church renews this teaching, proclaiming that the Kingdom of God is coming and will endure forever.”

Following the Angelus prayer on Sunday, the pope also prayed for young people…
items.t: Pope appeals for peace on Christ the King, dines with Rome’s poor families

items.title: Pope appeals for aid as ‘Super El Niño’ drives severe weather conditions across Asia-Pacific
items.summary:
Pope Leo XIV appealed for those suffering from a severe drought across Asia and Oceania, as emergency aid workers continue their work to alleviate conditions of food insecurity and economic hardship.

The U.N.’s Office of Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs says the El Niño-driven conditions could compound existing vulnerabilities across vast swathes of the Asia-Pacific region.

OCHA says as many as 190 million children face heightened risks to food and water security, general nutrition and health, as well as shelter, and education.

“My thoughts and prayers go out to the people of Papua New Guinea and other Pacific countries affected by drought,” the pontiff said Sunday after praying the Angelus with pilgrims and tourists gathered in St. Peter’s Square.

All 22 provinces of Papua New Guinea are currently facing emergency drought conditions, while experts are warning that this year’s El Niño phenomenon is driving severe weather across Asia and the Pacific.

The pope expressed his “closeness to all those suffering as a result of this emergency,” and offered his “gratitude to those working to assist the most severely affected.”

The U.N.’s Food and Agriculture Organization participated in an emergency meeting for Papua New Guinea in late October.

Earlier this month the OCHA issued a forecast saying experts expect humanitarian impacts to unfold in three successive waves over the next six months.

Weather experts say this year’s “Super El Niño” effect driving both drought and severe storm activity.
